plannerAnswers.question: What did you like most about this prompt?
plannerAnswers.answer: The 'This computer' section. It says what the machine has, what it lacks and which stand-in to use for each gap (a stubbed pad, phone profiles, reading audio levels, two pages for a second player), so I could test claims here instead of guessing, and the plan could pass exact recipes to builders. I also liked that the creative choices (genre, camera, stack beyond the engine) were left open while the product requirements (attract mode, dev sliders, 10-foot UI, music at 10%, one-command tests) were concrete and checkable, which made it clear what the plan had to cover.

plannerAnswers.question: What was confusing?
plannerAnswers.answer: Three things. First, the Tech Stack line points at dist/handoff, but that folder's README says real 3D is not in it and sends you to the repository. A source that needs a real over-the-shoulder camera can't really be built from the linked folder alone, and it took reading to establish that the add-on counts as the same engine. Second, the Multiplayer line says to follow the hub docs 'as well as for the game on its own', while those docs only cover sessions and say a game outside a session is unaffected. I couldn't tell whether that meant 'it must also run standalone' or 'it needs multiplayer standalone', so the plan covers both with solo and couch split-screen, and says why. Third, 'capture its world, characters, themes' next to 'an original game' doesn't say how close is too close. I took mechanics and tone as fair and made every name, place, character, level and tune new. A smaller point: the 3D engine's docs say 'served, not double-clicked' while TASK.md prefers file://, which I only settled by testing a bundled build.

plannerAnswers.question: What was the hardest thing to do?
plannerAnswers.answer: Writing a plan for builders I can't talk to and whose strength I don't know, so it had to be specific enough to follow, whole at any stopping point, and honest about what was proven. That meant a build order and a cut list that keep the game complete, not just a design. Technically, the hardest part was finding out which assumptions were false before a builder hit them: the engine's check tool falsely fails on real 3D, world.dispose() crashes on WebGPU (a WebGL-only test suite would never catch it), the Humanoid looks crude up close, and the standard menus are unreadable at 10 feet and ignore mouse hover until adjusted. Two of those contradicted things I had already written in the plan. Creatively, the hard part was staying true to what makes the source distinctive while keeping every specific original, which is where the wine-country premise came from.

plannerAnswers.question: What would you change in this prompt?
plannerAnswers.answer: State the Tech Stack for 3D sources directly, by naming E.World3D, or include the 3D add-on, its vendor folder and its kits in the handoff package, so the linked folder is enough. Pin the engine to a commit for each batch, or say that main moves: it went from v0.88.0 to v0.89.1 while I was working, and a plan's recipes are only as good as the version they were checked on. Reword the Multiplayer line to say which of the two meanings it wants. Give a rough target length in minutes for the demo, since 'long enough to show ALL features' can mean 15 minutes or 2 hours and it drives the whole scope. Tell the planner whether prototyping is expected and whether builders receive only PLAN.md, because I put every recipe inside the plan on that assumption. Also fix a few things outside the prompt that builders will trip on: the handoff README's 'npx playwright install' contradicts TASK.md's ban, tools/check.mjs reports false failures on World3D games, world.dispose() needs the patch in the plan, and { tv: true } could be the default for a game that declares itself controller-first.
